title: Hidden engines of monster supernovae revealed by NASA's Fermi telescope
summary:
Superluminous supernovae are the universe's most brilliant stellar explosions, shining at least 10 times brighter than ordinary supernovae. Since their discovery two decades ago, astronomers have debated what fuels them. Now, an international team using NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has found compelling evidence: magnetars. These are neutron stars with magnetic fields so intense—up to 1,000 times stronger than a typical neutron star—that they can energize a supernova from within.

The breakthrough came from SN 2017egm, a superluminous supernova in the galaxy NGC 3191, about 440 million light-years away. Despite the vast distance, it's one of the closest such events ever observed. Fermi's Large Area Telescope detected gamma rays from the supernova months after the initial explosion. "For nearly 20 years, astronomers have searched Fermi data for gamma-ray signals from thousands of supernovae, and while a few intriguing hints have been reported, none were definitive until now," said lead author Fabio Acero of CNRS and the University of Paris-Saclay.

The team compared the gamma-ray and visible light signals with theoretical models. A model by Indrek Vurm and Brian Metzger, which simulates a newborn magnetar spinning several hundred times per second, matched the observations best. The rapidly rotating magnetar generates a wind of electrons and positrons (antimatter electrons), creating a magnetar wind nebula. Inside this nebula, particle collisions produce gamma rays, but much of that energy is initially trapped by the supernova debris, converted to visible light, and only leaks out months later as the debris expands and cools. "About three months after the collapse, the gamma rays can begin to leak out," Acero explained.

The findings not only solve a long-standing mystery but also open a new observational window. The team predicts that the upcoming Cerenkov Telescope Array Observatory could detect similar events up to 500 million light-years away with just 50 hours of observation. This means we may soon be able to routinely study the hidden engines of the universe's most powerful explosions, probing the extreme physics of magnetars and the deaths of massive stars.
why_it_matters: Unlocking the power source of the universe's brightest explosions helps us understand the extreme physics of neutron stars and might eventually shed light on the origin of heavy elements like gold, which are forged in such cataclysmic events.

background_read: Superluminous supernovae, discovered in the late 1990s, are cosmic explosions that can briefly outshine entire galaxies. Their extraordinary brightness demanded a special power source. The leading candidate has been a magnetar — a newborn neutron star with a magnetic field a thousand trillion times stronger than a refrigerator magnet (first theorized in 1992 by Robert Duncan and Christopher Thompson). However, proof was elusive because the gamma rays emitted by the magnetar's wind nebula are initially trapped by the supernova debris. NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope (launched in 2008 to scan the sky in high-energy light) had scoured data from thousands of supernovae without a clear signal until it observed SN 2017egm, in the galaxy NGC 3191, 440 million light-years away. The detection confirms the magnetar model. In the future, the Cerenkov Telescope Array Observatory (a planned global network of gamma-ray telescopes) could spot many more such events, turning rare detections into routine study.

perspectives.description: The detection is a triumph of persistence, finally confirming the magnetar model that had been on the table for over 20 years. It paves the way for routine gamma-ray studies of supernova engines, deepening our knowledge of stellar death and extreme magnetic fields.

SN 2017egm is just one supernova, and while the model fits well, alternative extreme scenarios could produce similar gamma-ray patterns. Relying on the aging Fermi telescope also means the pace of discovery could slow until CTA becomes fully operational.

Supernova research has always advanced through combining visible, radio, and X-ray observations; gamma rays were the missing piece. The study highlights how long it can take for theory and observation to align, and how radiation trapping by debris is a universal feature of dense explosions.

perspectives.perspective: A new era of magnetar hunting
perspectives.description: With the Cerenkov Telescope Array expected to begin operations in the 2020s, astronomers will scan dozens more supernovae for magnetar wind nebulae. This could refine models, reveal new engine types, and revolutionize our understanding of cosmic magnetic fields and the birth of black holes.
